### 1. Definition & Essential Characteristics of an Algorithm [3 Marks]

An **algorithm** is a finite, ordered sequence of definite (unambiguous) and effective computational steps that transforms zero or more well-defined **inputs** into at least one desired **output**.
- **Input & Output:** Accepts `≥ 0` external inputs and produces `≥ 1` well-defined result.
- **Definiteness:** Every instruction has one exact, unambiguous meaning.
- **Finiteness:** Guaranteed to terminate after a finite number of steps on all valid inputs.
- **Effectiveness:** Every elementary operation is feasible in finite time.
- **Mini-Example (`MAX(a, b)`):** `(1) Read a, b;  (2) If a > b return a else return b;  (3) Stop.`

### 2. Complexity of an Algorithm [3 Marks]

**Algorithm complexity** quantifies the computational resources consumed as input size `n → ∞`, independent of hardware speed:

> [!COMPARE] Time Complexity vs Space Complexity
> | Parameter | Time Complexity `T(n)` | Space Complexity `S(n)` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Resource Measured** | Count of **elementary CPU steps** (comparisons, swaps, arithmetic). | **Working RAM** (`fixed part c + auxiliary/stack space S_P(n)`). |
> | **Cases Analysed** | **Best** (`min`), **Average** (expected), and **Worst** (`max`) cases. | Peak auxiliary + recursion stack footprint. |
> | **Concrete Example** | Linear Search `O(n)`; Binary Search `O(log n)`; Merge Sort `Θ(n log n)`. | Iterative Binary Search `O(1)`; Merge Sort `Θ(n)`. |

- **Asymptotic Growth Classes:** Expressed via **Big-O** (upper), **Big-Ω** (lower), and **Big-Θ** (tight): `O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)`.

### 1. Optimized Bubble Sort Algorithm [3 Marks]

**Bubble Sort** repeatedly steps through `A[0..n−1]`, comparing adjacent pairs `(A[j], A[j+1])` and swapping them whenever `A[j] > A[j+1]`. After pass `i`, the `(i+1)`-th largest key settles at `A[n − 1 − i]`. Adding a boolean `swapped` flag achieves early termination when the array becomes sorted:

```text
BUBBLE_SORT(A, n):
  for i <- 0 to n - 2 do
      swapped <- false
      for j <- 0 to n - i - 2 do
          if A[j] > A[j + 1] then
              temp <- A[j]
              A[j] <- A[j + 1]
              A[j + 1] <- temp
              swapped <- true
      if swapped == false then
          break    // Early exit: zero inversions remain
  return A
```

### 2. Worked Pass Trace on `A = [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]` (`n = 5`) [2 Marks]

| Pass | Comparisons & Swaps Executed | Array State After Pass |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | `(5,1)` swap, `(5,4)` swap, `(5,2)` swap, `(5,8)` keep | `[1, 4, 2, 5 ¦` **`8`**`]` |
| **2** | `(1,4)` keep, `(4,2)` swap, `(4,5)` keep | `[1, 2, 4 ¦` **`5, 8`**`]` |
| **3** | `(1,2)` keep, `(2,4)` keep → `swapped = false`, **break** | **`[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]`** |

### 3. Complexity & Properties [1 Mark]

- **Time Complexity:** Best case **`Θ(n)`** (already sorted, `1` pass); Average & Worst case **`Θ(n²)`** (`n(n − 1)/2` comparisons/swaps on reverse-sorted input).
- **Space & Stability:** **`O(1)`** auxiliary space (in-place) and **Stable** (strict `>` never swaps equal keys).

### a) Colpitts Oscillator — Circuit, Operation, and Resonant Frequency [4 Marks]

A **Colpitts oscillator** is an RF sinusoidal **LC feedback oscillator** (`~10 kHz` to `300 MHz`) consisting of a common-emitter BJT (or op-amp) inverting amplifier (`180°` phase shift) coupled to a **capacitive voltage-divider tank network** formed by **one inductor `L` in parallel with two series capacitors `C₁` and `C₂`** (contributing the remaining `180°` phase shift for `360°` regenerative feedback):

```ascii
                    +Vcc
                     |
                    [Rc]----> Coupling Cap Cc ----> Sinusoidal RF Output
                     |                              |
      Bias R1/R2 --> B   C -------------------------+----+
                     | /                                 |
                   BJT (CE: 180 deg)                    [C1]
                     | \                                 |
                     E --[Re]-- GND        Tank (L)      +---> GND (Center tap)
                     |                       ( )         |
                     +--- Feedback <---------+----------+----[C2]---+
                          (180 deg)          |______________________|
```

### 1. General Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm Template [3 Marks]

**Divide and Conquer (`D&C`)** solves a problem instance `P` of size `n` by decomposing it into independent sub-instances of the same problem type:

```text
DIVIDE_AND_CONQUER(P):
  if SMALL(P) then
      return SOLVE_DIRECTLY(P)             // Base case (e.g., n <= 1 in O(1))
  Divide P into smaller disjoint subproblems P1, P2, ..., Pa (each of size ~ n/b)
  for i <- 1 to a do
      Si <- DIVIDE_AND_CONQUER(Pi)         // Conquer recursively
  return COMBINE(S1, S2, ..., Sa)          // Stitch sub-solutions
```

### 2. Detailed Three-Stage Explanation & Master Recurrence [3 Marks]

1. **Divide:** Partition the input of size `n` into `a ≥ 1` smaller, **non-overlapping** subproblems of size `n / b`.
2. **Conquer:** Solve each subproblem recursively; once subproblem size reaches a trivial threshold (`n ≤ n₀`), compute the base answer directly.
3. **Combine:** Merge the subproblem outputs `S₁..S_a` into the final answer for `P`.

> [!FORMULA] Master Divide-and-Conquer Recurrence
> `T(n) = a · T(n / b) + f(n)`, where `f(n) = D(n) + C(n)` is the divide + combine overhead.

- **Canonical D&C Algorithms:**
  - **Merge Sort:** `a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = Θ(n)` → **`T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n)`**.
  - **Binary Search:** `a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = O(1)` → **`T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n)`**.
  - **Quick Sort:** In-place partition (`D(n) = Θ(n)`, `C(n) = O(1)`) → **`Θ(n log n)`** average.
  - **Strassen's Matrix Multiplication:** `7` recursive `n/2 × n/2` products → **`O(n^2.81)`** (beating `O(n³)`).

### 1. Kruskal's Greedy MST Algorithm [2 Marks]

```text
MST_KRUSKAL(G, w):
  T <- EMPTY_SET
  for each vertex v in G.V do MAKE_SET(v)     // |V| singleton trees
  Sort all edges of G.E in non-decreasing order of weight w
  for each edge (u, v) in sorted G.E do
      if FIND_SET(u) != FIND_SET(v) then      // Safe edge: no cycle
          T <- T U {(u, v)}
          UNION(u, v)
          if |T| == |G.V| - 1 then break
  return T
```

- **Complexity:** **`O(E log E) = O(E log V)`** (dominated by edge sorting; Disjoint-Set operations run in `O(α(V))` amortized).

### a) Time Complexity Derivation of the Doubling `while` Loop [4 Marks]

Given `i = 1; while (i <= n) { printf("CST\n"); i = i * 2; }`, variable `i` **doubles (`× 2`)** on every iteration rather than incrementing by `1`:

| Iteration # | Value of `i` Tested (`i ≤ n`) | Exponential Form | Next `i = i * 2` |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `1` | `1` | `2⁰` | `2¹` |
| `2` | `2` | `2¹` | `2²` |
| `3` | `4` | `2²` | `2³` |
| `…` | `…` | `…` | `…` |
| `k + 1` | `2^k ≤ n` | `2^k` | `2^(k+1) > n` *(terminates)* |

- **Solving Stopping Condition `2^k ≤ n < 2^(k+1)`:** Taking `log₂` across both sides gives `k ≤ log₂ n < k + 1`, so `k = ⌊log₂ n⌋` (e.g., for `n = 16`, `i` takes values `1, 2, 4, 8, 16` = `⌊log₂ 16⌋ + 1 = 5` iterations before `32 > 16` halts).
- **Total Iterations:** `k + 1 = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1` (`O(1)` `printf` + multiplication work per iteration) → **Time Complexity = `Θ(log n)`** (or **`O(log n)`**), Auxiliary Space = **`O(1)`**.

### b) Basic Concept of the Divide and Conquer Algorithmic Model [4 Marks]

**Divide and Conquer (`D&C`)** decomposes a problem of size `n` recursively in three distinct stages:
1. **Divide:** Partition the input into `a ≥ 1` smaller, **independent** subproblems of size `n / b`.
2. **Conquer:** Solve the subproblems recursively (solving small base cases directly in `O(1)`).
3. **Combine:** Merge the subproblem answers to form the solution to the original problem.
- **Master Recurrence:** **`T(n) = a · T(n / b) + f(n)`**, where `f(n)` is the cost of dividing + combining.
- **Canonical Examples:** **Merge Sort** (`2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n)`), **Quick Sort** (`Θ(n log n)` average), and **Binary Search** (`T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n)`).

### a) Conditions When Linear Search Should Be Considered [2 Marks]

1. **Unsorted Data:** Input array is unordered and no prior sort index exists.
2. **Sequential-Access Structures:** Data resides in a **singly/doubly linked list** or input stream lacking `O(1)` random indexing.
3. **Small `n` or Single Query:** Dataset is tiny (`n ≲ 32`, cache-line scan beats branch overhead) or searched only once (where sorting first in `Θ(n log n)` would cost more than one `O(n)` scan).

### b.i) Algorithm for Binary Search (`A[0..n−1]` Sorted Ascending) [4 Marks]

```text
BINARY_SEARCH(A, n, key):
  low <- 0
  high <- n - 1
  while low <= high do
      mid <- low + floor((high - low) / 2)
      if A[mid] == key then
          return mid            // Match found at index mid
      else if A[mid] < key then
          low <- mid + 1        // Search upper half
      else
          high <- mid - 1       // Search lower half
  return -1                     // Key absent
```

### b.ii) Why Binary Search Complexity Is `O(log n)` [2 Marks]

- **Active Range Halving:** Initially `n` elements are active. After comparison `1`, at most `⌊n/2⌋` remain; after comparison `2`, at most `⌊n/2²⌋`; after comparison `k`, at most **`⌊n / 2^k⌋`** elements remain.
- **Worst-Case Bound:** The search terminates no later than when the active range shrinks below `1` element (`n / 2^k < 1 ⇒ 2^k > n ⇒ k > log₂ n`), requiring at most **`⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 = O(log n)`** comparisons (`T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)`) and **`O(1)`** extra space (for `n = 1,024`, at most `11` comparisons vs `1,024` in Linear Search).

### a) Significance & Advantages of Height-Balancing a Binary Search Tree [4 Marks]

Every BST operation (`SEARCH`, `INSERT`, `DELETE`, `MIN`, `SUCCESSOR`) runs in **`O(h)`** time proportional to tree height `h`:
- **Degenerate Unbalanced Hazard:** Inserting sorted or nearly sorted keys (`10, 20, 30, 40`) into an ordinary BST produces a skewed chain of height **`h = n − 1`**, degrading all operations to **`O(n)`** linear search.
- **Height-Balance Invariant (`AVL` / `Red-Black`):** Maintaining **`|BF(x)| = |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1`** via `O(1)` local rotations (`LL, RR, LR, RL`) keeps tree height strictly bounded at **`h ≤ 1.44 log₂(n + 2) = Θ(log n)`**.

> [!COMPARE] Unbalanced BST vs Height-Balanced BST (AVL)
> | Parameter | Unbalanced BST | Height-Balanced BST (AVL) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Worst-Case Height `h`** | `n − 1` (`Θ(n)` skewed chain) | **`Θ(log n)`** |
> | **Worst-Case Search / Insert / Delete** | **`O(n)`** | **`O(log n)`** guaranteed |
> | **Predictable Real-Time Latency** | Vulnerable to sorted-input spikes | Deterministic logarithmic bound |

### b) Pseudocode of `INSERT` Operation in a Binary Search Tree [4 Marks]

```text
BST_INSERT(root, key):
  if root == NULL then
      return NEW_NODE(key)                    // Attach new leaf node
  if key < root.key then
      root.left <- BST_INSERT(root.left, key) // Branch into left subtree
  else if key > root.key then
      root.right <- BST_INSERT(root.right, key) // Branch into right subtree
  // (Duplicate keys ignored or handled per policy)
  return root
```

- **Complexity:** Traverses a single root-to-leaf path in **`O(h)`** time (`O(log n)` on a height-balanced AVL/Red-Black BST vs `O(n)` worst-case on a skewed BST) and `O(h)` recursion stack (`O(1)` if implemented iteratively).

### a) How Prim's Algorithm Works [3 Marks]

**Prim's greedy MST algorithm** grows a **single connected tree `T`** vertex-by-vertex in `O(E log V)` time:
1. **Initialize:** Pick any start vertex `r`, set `key[r] = 0`, `key[v] = ∞` (`∀ v ≠ r`), and place all vertices in Min-Priority Queue `Q`.
2. **Greedy Cut Step:** Extract vertex `u` with minimum `key[u]` from `Q` (adding edge `(parent[u], u)` to the MST).
3. **Update Frontier:** For every neighbor `v ∈ Adj[u]` still in `Q`, if `w(u, v) < key[v]`, set `key[v] ← w(u, v)` and `parent[v] ← u`. Repeat until `Q = ∅` (`|V| − 1` edges added).

### 1. Principle & Pseudocode of Merge Sort [3 Marks]

**Merge Sort** is a canonical **Divide and Conquer** sorting algorithm: (1) **Divide** `A[left..right]` at `mid = ⌊(left + right)/2⌋`; (2) **Conquer** both halves recursively; (3) **Combine** the two sorted halves in `Θ(n)` linear time using two-finger `MERGE`:

```text
MERGE_SORT(A, left, right):
  if left < right then
      mid <- left + floor((right - left) / 2)
      MERGE_SORT(A, left, mid)
      MERGE_SORT(A, mid + 1, right)
      MERGE(A, left, mid, right)

MERGE(A, left, mid, right):
  Copy A[left..mid] -> L[0..n1-1] and A[mid+1..right] -> R[0..n2-1]
  i <- 0;  j <- 0;  k <- left
  while i < n1 and j < n2 do
      if L[i] <= R[j] then A[k++] <- L[i++]   // '<=' preserves stability
      else                 A[k++] <- R[j++]
  Copy any remaining elements of L[] or R[] into A[k..right]
```

### a) Dijkstra's Single-Source Shortest-Path (`SSSP`) Algorithm [5 Marks]

Precondition: Weighted graph `G = (V, E)` with **non-negative edge weights (`w(u, v) ≥ 0`)** and source `s`:

```text
DIJKSTRA(G, w, s):
  for each vertex v in G.V do
      dist[v] <- INFINITY
      parent[v] <- NIL
  dist[s] <- 0
  S <- EMPTY_SET                         // Settled vertices
  Q <- BUILD_MIN_HEAP(G.V)               // Priority queue keyed by dist[v]
  while Q is not empty do
      u <- EXTRACT_MIN(Q)                // Greedily pick closest unsettled u
      S <- S U {u}
      for each edge (u, v) in Adj[u] do  // Edge relaxation
          if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] then
              dist[v] <- dist[u] + w(u, v)
              parent[v] <- u
              DECREASE_KEY(Q, v, dist[v])
```

### a) Rabin–Karp String-Matching Algorithm [6 Marks]

Given text `T[0..n−1]`, pattern `P[0..m−1]`, alphabet radix `d` (e.g., `d = 256` for ASCII), and prime modulus `q`, **Rabin–Karp** slides an `O(1)` **modular rolling hash** across `T`:

```text
RABIN_KARP_MATCHER(T, P, d, q):
  n <- length(T);  m <- length(P)
  h <- d^(m - 1) mod q                   // Weight of leading digit
  p <- 0;  t0 <- 0
  for i <- 0 to m - 1 do                 // Horner preprocessing in Theta(m)
      p  <- (d * p  + P[i]) mod q
      t0 <- (d * t0 + T[i]) mod q
  for s <- 0 to n - m do                 // Slide window across text
      if p == ts then                    // Hash hit: verify characters!
          if P[0..m-1] == T[s..s+m-1] then
              print "Pattern occurs with shift", s
      if s < n - m then                  // O(1) rolling update for next shift
          ts+1 <- (d * (ts - T[s] * h) + T[s + m]) mod q
          if ts+1 < 0 then ts+1 <- ts+1 + q
```

- **Spurious-Hit Verification:** Because two unequal substrings can collide modulo `q` (`ts == p` while `T[s..s+m−1] ≠ P`), exact character comparison is mandatory on hash equality.
- **Worked Mini-Trace (`T = "2359023141526739921"`, `P = "31415"`, `d = 10`, `q = 13`):** `p = 31415 mod 13 = 7`. Window `"67399"` gives `67399 mod 13 = 7` (*spurious hit*, rejected on char check), while window **`"31415"` at `s = 6`** gives `7 == 7` and verifies as an **exact match**!

### a) Prim's Algorithm for Minimum Spanning Tree (`MST`) [4 Marks]

### a) Significance of Linear-Time Sorting Algorithms [2 Marks]

- **Breaking the `Ω(n log n)` Decision-Tree Barrier:** Every comparison-based sort (Merge, Quick, Heap) requires at least `⌈log₂(n!)⌉ = Ω(n log n)` comparisons in the worst case.

1. **Restricted Input Domain:** Cannot sort arbitrary user-defined objects via a comparator alone — requires bounded integers (`0..k`), fixed-length strings/digits, or known probability distributions.
2. **Extra Memory Overhead (`O(n + k)`):** Not in-place; if range `k ≫ n` (e.g., `k = n²`), Counting Sort wastes `O(n²)` space and time.
3. **Distribution Sensitivity:** Bucket Sort degrades to **`O(n²)`** worst case (or `O(n log n)`) if skewed data clusters all `n` keys into one bucket.

### a) Recursive Binary Search Algorithm & Explanation [4 Marks]

```text
REC_BINARY_SEARCH(A, low, high, key):
  if low > high then
      return -1                             // Base case: empty range (absent)
  mid <- low + floor((high - low) / 2)      // Overflow-safe midpoint
  if A[mid] == key then
      return mid                            // Base case: target matched
  else if key < A[mid] then
      return REC_BINARY_SEARCH(A, low, mid - 1, key)   // Recurse left half
  else
      return REC_BINARY_SEARCH(A, mid + 1, high, key)  // Recurse right half
```

- **Working:** Invoked initially as `REC_BINARY_SEARCH(A, 0, n − 1, key)`. Because `A` is sorted in ascending order, comparing `key` with `A[mid]` deterministically eliminates half of the remaining candidates on every recursive call until either `A[mid] == key` or `low > high`.

### b) Is Binary Search Useful on an Unsorted Array? [1 Mark]

- **No.** On an unsorted array, `key < A[mid]` gives **no guarantee** that `key` is absent from the right half (so discarding half can miss `key`), and sorting first (`Θ(n log n)`) for a single query is slower than a direct `O(n)` Linear Search.

### c) Time & Space Complexity Derivation [3 Marks]

> [!FORMULA] Binary Search Recurrence
> `T(n) = T(n / 2) + c`, with `T(1) = c`.

- **Unrolling (`n = 2^k ⇒ k = log₂ n`):**
  `T(n) = T(n/2) + c = T(n/4) + 2c = … = T(n / 2^k) + k·c = T(1) + c·log₂ n =` **`O(log n)`**.
- **Summary:** Best case **`O(1)`** (`A[mid] == key` on call `1`); Average & Worst case **`Θ(log n)`** time; Auxiliary space **`O(log n)`** recursion call stack (`O(1)` if rewritten iteratively).

### a) What is Hashing? [2 Marks]

**Hashing** is an address-calculation technique that maps an arbitrary search key `k` from a large key universe `U` directly into a bounded array index `0..m−1` via a deterministic **hash function `h(k)`**, achieving **`O(1)` expected-time** insertion, lookup, and deletion instead of `O(n)` or `O(log n)` key comparisons.

### a) Bellman–Ford Single-Source Shortest-Path Algorithm [4 Marks]

Unlike Dijkstra's algorithm, **Bellman–Ford** handles **negative edge weights** and detects reachable **negative-weight cycles** in **`Θ(V · E)`** time:

```text
BELLMAN_FORD(G, w, s):
  for each vertex v in G.V do
      dist[v] <- INFINITY;  parent[v] <- NIL
  dist[s] <- 0
  for pass <- 1 to |G.V| - 1 do                 // Relax all edges |V|-1 times
      for each directed edge (u, v) in G.E do
          if dist[u] != INFINITY and dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] then
              dist[v] <- dist[u] + w(u, v)
              parent[v] <- u
  for each directed edge (u, v) in G.E do       // |V|-th negative-cycle check
      if dist[u] != INFINITY and dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] then
          return FALSE                          // Negative-weight cycle exists!
  return TRUE
```

### a) Selection Sort Algorithm & Worked Example [4 Marks]

**Selection Sort** partitions `A[0..n−1]` into a sorted prefix `A[0..i−1]` and an unsorted suffix `A[i..n−1]`. In pass `i`, it scans `A[i..n−1]` to locate the **minimum element's index `min_idx`** and swaps `A[i] ↔ A[min_idx]` (performing **at most `n − 1` swaps** total):

```text
SELECTION_SORT(A, n):
  for i <- 0 to n - 2 do
      min_idx <- i
      for j <- i + 1 to n - 1 do
          if A[j] < A[min_idx] then min_idx <- j
      swap(A[i], A[min_idx])
```

### a) Iterative Binary Search Algorithm [3 Marks]

Precondition: Array `A[0..n−1]` is sorted in ascending order (`O(log n)` worst-case time, `O(1)` space):

```text
BINARY_SEARCH(A, n, key):
  low <- 0
  high <- n - 1
  while low <= high do
      mid <- low + floor((high - low) / 2)
      if A[mid] == key then
          return mid            // Target found at index mid
      else if key < A[mid] then
          high <- mid - 1       // Discard right half
      else
          low <- mid + 1        // Discard left half
  return -1                     // Target absent
```

### b) Collision in Hashing & Collision Resolution Techniques [5 Marks]

A **hash collision** occurs when two distinct keys `k₁ ≠ k₂` produce the identical bucket address `h(k₁) == h(k₂)` in table `T[0..m−1]` (inevitable whenever key universe `|U| > m` by the Pigeonhole Principle).

- **1. Separate Chaining (*Open Hashing*):**
  - Each table slot `T[i]` heads a **singly/doubly linked list** of all keys hashing to `i`.
  - Supports load factor `α = n/m > 1` gracefully with `O(1 + α)` expected search/insert and straightforward pointer deletion.
- **2. Open Addressing (*Closed Hashing* — `α ≤ 1`, all keys stored inside `T`):**
  Probe sequence `h(k, i) = (h₁(k) + f(i)) mod m` for `i = 0, 1, …, m − 1`:
  - **Linear Probing (`f(i) = i`):** Probes `(h₁(k) + i) mod m` sequentially; cache-friendly, but suffers from **primary clustering** (long contiguous runs merge and widen).
  - **Quadratic Probing (`f(i) = c₁i + c₂i²`):** Jumps quadratically `(h₁(k) + i²) mod m`, eliminating primary clustering while leaving mild **secondary clustering** among keys sharing `h₁(k)`.
  - **Double Hashing (`f(i) = i · h₂(k)`):** Uses a second independent non-zero hash `h₂(k)` (coprime to `m`, e.g., `R − (k mod R)`), giving key-specific step sizes and **eliminating both primary and secondary clustering**.

### a) Tries (Prefix Trees) & How They Store Strings [3 Marks]

A **Trie** (*retrieval / prefix tree*) is a multi-way rooted tree specialized for storing a dynamic set of strings over an alphabet `Σ`:
- **Character-Along-Edge Path:** Unlike a BST (which stores whole keys at nodes), each edge from parent to child represents **one character**, so a node's implicit prefix equals the characters along its root-to-node path.
- **Shared Prefixes & `isEndOfWord` Flag:** Words sharing a common prefix (e.g., `"do"`, `"doll"`, `"dork"`, `"dorm"`) **share the exact same prefix nodes**, saving space and supporting instant autocomplete; a boolean **`isEnd` (`*`)** flag marks complete dictionary words.

### b) Trie Construction & Search Efficiency (`*` = `isEndOfWord = true`) [5 Marks]

```ascii

                     /     |      \
                   b       d        s
                   |       |        |
                   a      o*        e
                  / \    /  \       |
                t*   l  l    r      n
                     |  |   / \    / \
                    l* l*  k*  m* d*  s
                                      |
                                      e*
```

  - **`"do"`** marks node `o*` as terminal while still branching downward to `l→l*` (`"doll"`) and `r→{k*, m*}` (`"dork"`, `"dorm"`).

### a) Knuth–Morris–Pratt (`KMP`) String Matching Algorithm [3 Marks]

Naive string matching backtracks text pointer `i` on mismatches (`O(n · m)` worst case). **KMP** achieves deterministic **`Θ(n + m)`** worst-case time in two phases:
1. **Pattern Preprocessing (`COMPUTE_LPS`, `Θ(m)`):** Builds `LPS[0..m−1]` (*Longest Proper Prefix of `P[0..j]` that is also a Suffix of `P[0..j]`*).
2. **Non-Backtracking Scan (`Θ(n)`):** Compares `T[i]` with `P[j]`. On match, increment both `i` and `j`. On mismatch: if `j > 0`, jump **`j ← LPS[j − 1]`** (**`i` never decrements!**) so already matched prefix characters are reused; if `j == 0`, increment `i`.

### a) Definition & Characteristics of a Good Algorithm [4 Marks]

An **algorithm** is a finite, ordered sequence of unambiguous, elementary computational steps that accepts well-defined input(s) and terminates with the required output(s).
- **1. Input:** Accepts zero or more externally supplied quantities (e.g., `gcd(a, b)` takes two non-negative integers).
- **2. Output:** Produces **at least one** well-defined result corresponding to the input.
- **3. Definiteness (Unambiguity):** Every step must be crystal clear with one exact meaning (e.g., `r ← a mod b`, never *"pick a small number"*).
- **4. Finiteness:** Must terminate after a **finite number of steps** for every valid input (e.g., Euclid's `GCD` decreases `b` strictly toward `0`).
- **5. Effectiveness:** Every operation must be basic enough to execute in finite time with pencil and paper.
- **Example — Euclid's GCD (`gcd(48, 18)`):** `(48, 18) → (18, 12) → (12, 6) → (6, 0)` → returns **`6`** in `3` finite, unambiguous modulo steps.

### b) Asymptotic Notations in Algorithm Analysis [4 Marks]

Asymptotic notations characterize growth rate `T(n)` for large `n` while ignoring machine-dependent constants and lower-order terms:

> [!COMPARE] Big-O vs Big-Omega (`Ω`) vs Big-Theta (`Θ`) Asymptotic Bounds
> | Parameter | Big-O (`O(g(n))`) | Big-Omega (`Ω(g(n))`) | Big-Theta (`Θ(g(n))`) |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **Bound Type** | **Asymptotic Upper Bound** (`≤`). | **Asymptotic Lower Bound** (`≥`). | **Asymptotically Tight Bound** (`=`). |
> | **Formal Inequality (`∀ n ≥ n₀`)** | `0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c · g(n)` (`c > 0`). | `0 ≤ c · g(n) ≤ f(n)` (`c > 0`). | `0 ≤ c₁·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂·g(n)`. |
> | **Typical Case Described** | Worst-case ceiling (e.g., Insertion Sort `O(n²)`). | Best-case / problem lower floor (`Ω(n)`). | Exact order when upper & lower match (Merge Sort `Θ(n log n)`). |

- **Strict Notations:** **Little-o (`o(g(n))`)** denotes a strict upper bound (`lim f(n)/g(n) = 0`, e.g., `2n = o(n²)`), and **Little-omega (`ω(g(n))`)** denotes a strict lower bound (`lim f(n)/g(n) = ∞`).

### a) Divide and Conquer Technique with Suitable Example [4 Marks]

**Divide and Conquer (`D&C`)** solves a problem of size `n` in three recursive phases:
1. **Divide:** Partition the original instance into `a ≥ 1` smaller, **disjoint (independent)** subproblems of size `n / b`.
2. **Conquer:** Solve each subproblem recursively (solving tiny base cases directly in `O(1)`).
3. **Combine:** Merge the subproblem solutions into the solution for the full input.

```ascii
[38, 27, 43, 3] --Divide--> [38, 27] & [43, 3] --Divide--> [38] [27] [43] [3]
                                                              |
[3, 27, 38, 43] <--Combine-- [27, 38] & [3, 43] <--Combine---+
```

- **Recurrence & Complexity (Merge Sort Example):** Splitting takes `O(1)`, conquering two halves takes `2T(n/2)`, and linear merging takes `Θ(n)`, yielding **`T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n)`**.

### b) Divide and Conquer vs Dynamic Programming [4 Marks]

> [!COMPARE] Divide and Conquer vs Dynamic Programming
> | Parameter | Divide and Conquer (`D&C`) | Dynamic Programming (`DP`) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Subproblem Structure** | Subproblems are **independent / non-overlapping**. | Subproblems **overlap heavily** (shared sub-instances). |
> | **Recomputation & Storage** | Each disjoint subproblem is solved once without a lookup table. | Solves each distinct subproblem **once** and caches it via **tabulation** or **memoization**. |
> | **Execution Direction** | Naturally **top-down recursive**. | Typically **bottom-up iterative** table filling (or top-down memoized). |
> | **Target Problem Class** | General decomposition (sorting, searching, matrix multiply). | **Optimization / counting** problems with *optimal substructure*. |
> | **Classic Examples** | **Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary Search, Strassen's**. | **`0/1` Knapsack, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford, LCS**. |

### a) Binary Search Algorithm & Worked Trace [5 Marks]

**Binary Search** applies decrease-and-conquer on a **sorted random-access array `A[0..n−1]`**, halving the active interval `[low..high]` on every comparison (`T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n)`):

```text
BINARY_SEARCH(A, n, key):
  low <- 0;  high <- n - 1
  while low <= high do
      mid <- low + floor((high - low) / 2)   // Prevents (low + high) integer overflow
      if A[mid] == key then return mid
      else if key < A[mid] then high <- mid - 1
      else low <- mid + 1
  return -1   // Key not found
```

- **Worked Example:** Search `key = 37` in sorted `A = [12, 25, 33, 37, 48, 57, 86, 92]` (`n = 8`):

| Step | `low` | `high` | `mid` | `A[mid]` | Comparison & Action |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **1** | `0` | `7` | `3` | `37` | `37 == A[3]` → **Found immediately at index `3`!** |

- *(Searching `key = 86` instead: Step 1 `mid = 3` (`86 > 37 → low = 4`); Step 2 `mid = 5` (`86 > 57 → low = 6`); Step 3 `mid = 6` (`A[6] == 86` → Found in `3 ≤ ⌈log₂ 8⌉` steps).)*

### a) Binary Search Tree (`BST`): Definition, Insertion, and Deletion [5 Marks]

A **Binary Search Tree (`BST`)** is a rooted binary tree where every node `x` satisfies the **BST ordering property**: all keys in `x.left` are **`< x.key`**, and all keys in `x.right` are **`> x.key`**.

- **1. BST Insertion (`O(h)`):** Compare new key `k` at root; branch left if `k < x.key` or right if `k > x.key` until reaching `NULL`, and attach `new Node(k)` as a leaf.
- **2. BST Deletion (`O(h)` — Three Exhaustive Structural Cases):**

```ascii
Case 1 (Leaf: del 20)     Case 2 (1 Child: del 30)    Case 3 (2 Children: del 50)
     30                        50                          50  --> replace with
    /  \   ==>   30           /  \    ==>    50           /  \     inorder successor 60:
  [20]  40         \       [30]   70        /  \        30    70        60
                    40        \           40    70           /  \      /  \
                               40                          [60]  80  30    70 (80)
```

  - **Case 1 — Leaf Node (`0` children):** Simply set parent's child pointer to `NULL` and free the node.
  - **Case 2 — One Child:** Bypass the deleted node by linking its single child directly to its parent.
  - **Case 3 — Two Children:** Locate the node's **inorder successor** (minimum key in `x.right`, or inorder predecessor in `x.left`), copy that key into `x`, and recursively delete the successor (which has at most `1` right child → reduces to Case 1 or 2).

### b) Significance of Balanced Binary Search Trees [3 Marks]

- **Preventing Skewed `O(n)` Degeneration:** Inserting pre-sorted keys (`10, 20, 30, 40, …`) into an unbalanced BST creates a degenerate linked chain of height **`h = n − 1`**, degrading search, insert, and delete from `O(log n)` to **`O(n)`**.
- **Guaranteed `O(log n)` Worst-Case Bounds:** Self-balancing BSTs (**AVL Trees** with `|BF| ≤ 1` and **Red-Black Trees** with black-height invariants) perform `O(1)` local rotations (`LL, RR, LR, RL`) during updates so tree height strictly satisfies **`h = Θ(log n)`** (`≤ 1.44 log₂ n` for AVL), ensuring predictable real-time lookup in databases, `std::map`, and OS schedulers.

A **collision** occurs when two distinct keys map to the same slot (`h(k₁) == h(k₂)`): > [!COMPARE] Separate Chaining vs Open Addressing Collision Resolution > | Parameter | Separate Chaining (Open Hashing) | Open Addressing (Closed Hashing) | > |---|---|---| > | **Storage Layout** | Each slot `T[i]` points to a **linked list (bucket chain)** of colliding keys. | All keys reside **directly inside table `T[0..m−1]`** (`α = n/m ≤ 1`). | > | **Probe / Resolution Rule** | Append/search along chain `T[h(k)]` (`O(1 + α)` average). | Probe sequence `h(k, i) = (h₁(k) + f(i)) mod m` for `i = 0, 1, 2, …`:
• **Linear Probing:** `f(i) = i` (*primary clustering*)
• **Quadratic Probing:** `f(i) = c₁i + c₂i²` (*secondary clustering*)
• **Double Hashing:** `f(i) = i · h₂(k)` (*minimal clustering*) | > | **Deletion Handling** | Standard linked-list node removal. | Requires lazy **`DELETED` tombstone** markers so probe chains stay intact. | ### b) Rabin-Karp String Matching Algorithm [4 Marks] Given text `T[0..n−1]` and pattern `P[0..m−1]` over alphabet radix `d` and prime modulus `q`, **Rabin-Karp** compares `P`'s hash `p` against each length-`m` window hash `t_s` of `T`: > [!FORMULA] Rolling Hash Recurrence (`O(1)` Window Slide) > `t_{s+1} = (d × (t_s − T[s] × h) + T[s + m]) mod q`, where `h = d^(m−1) mod q`. 1. **Preprocessing (`Θ(m)`):** Compute `p` for `P[0..m−1]` and initial window `t₀` for `T[0..m−1]` via Horner's rule. 2. **Sliding & Spurious-Hit Verification:** For shift `s = 0..n−m`: if `t_s ≠ p`, reject in `O(1)`; if `t_s == p` (*hash hit*), compare `T[s..s+m−1]` vs `P[0..m−1]` character-by-character to filter out **spurious hits** (hash collisions). 3. **Worked Mini-Trace (`T = "31415"`, `P = "15"`, `d = 10`, `q = 13`):** `p = 15 mod 13 = 2`. Windows: `"31"→5 ≠ 2`, `"14"→1 ≠ 2`, `"41"→2 == 2` (*spurious hit*: `"41" ≠ "15"`), `"15"→2 == 2` (*exact match at shift `s = 3`!*). 4. **Complexity:** Average **`O(n + m)`**; Worst case **`O(n · m)`** under pathological hash collisions.

### a) Definition of Graph & Major Graph Types [3 Marks]

A **graph** `G = (V, E)` consists of a finite non-empty set of **vertices (nodes) `V`** and a set of **edges `E`** connecting vertex pairs:
- **1. Undirected vs Directed (*Digraph*):** Unordered pairs `{u, v}` (Facebook friendships) vs ordered arcs `(u → v)` (web hyperlinks).
- **2. Weighted Graph:** Associates a real cost `w(e)` with each edge (road network distances).
- **3. Connected vs Disconnected:** Path exists between every vertex pair vs multiple isolated components.
- **4. Cyclic vs Acyclic (`DAG`):** Contains at least one closed simple cycle vs zero directed cycles (task dependency `DAG`).
- **5. Complete Graph (`Kₙ`) & Bipartite Graph:** Every pair connected (`n(n − 1)/2` edges) vs vertices split into `V₁ ∪ V₂` with edges strictly between `V₁` and `V₂`.

### b) Prim's Algorithm for Minimum Spanning Tree (`MST`) [5 Marks]

Given a connected, undirected weighted graph `G = (V, E)`, **Prim's greedy algorithm** grows a single tree `T` starting from an arbitrary root `r`, repeatedly adding the **minimum-weight safe edge `(u, v)`** crossing the cut `(T, V − T)` until `|T| = |V|`:
- **Algorithm Steps:** Initialize `key[v] = ∞`, `parent[v] = NIL` for all `v`, set `key[r] = 0`, and push all vertices into a Min-Priority Queue `Q`. While `Q ≠ ∅`: extract `u = EXTRACT_MIN(Q)`, and for every `(u, v) ∈ Adj[u]` with `v ∈ Q` and `w(u, v) < key[v]`, update `parent[v] ← u` and `key[v] ← w(u, v)`. **Complexity:** **`O(E log V)`** with binary heap (`O(V²)` with array).

```ascii
    (A)---2---(B)
     | \       |         Start at A:
     6   3     1         Step 1: Pick (A, B) w=2   [Tree: {A, B}]
     |     \   |         Step 2: Pick (B, D) w=1   [Tree: {A, B, D}]
    (C)---4---(D)        Step 3: Pick (C, D) w=4   [Tree: {A, B, D, C}]
```

| Step | Tree Set `T` | Candidate Cut Edges | Chosen Min Edge | Weight |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | `{A}` | `(A,B)=2, (A,D)=3, (A,C)=6` | **`(A, B)`** | `2` |
| **2** | `{A, B}` | `(B,D)=1, (A,D)=3, (A,C)=6` | **`(B, D)`** | `1` |
| **3** | `{A, B, D}` | `(D,C)=4, (A,C)=6` (`(A,D)=3` internal) | **`(D, C)`** | `4` |

- **Total MST Cost:** `2 + 1 + 4 =` **`7`** (`|V| − 1 = 3` edges).

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 5 marks + b) 3 marks

### a) Dijkstra's Single-Source Shortest Path (`SSSP`) Algorithm [5 Marks]

For a weighted graph `G = (V, E)` with **non-negative edge weights (`w(u, v) ≥ 0`)**, **Dijkstra's greedy algorithm** computes shortest-path distances `dist[v]` from source `s` to all vertices:

> [!FORMULA] Edge Relaxation Rule
> `RELAX(u, v, w): if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] then dist[v] ← dist[u] + w(u, v); parent[v] ← u`

1. **Initialization:** Set `dist[s] = 0`, `dist[v] = ∞` (`∀ v ≠ s`), settled set `S = ∅`, and insert `V` into Min-Heap `Q`.
2. **Greedy Selection & Relaxation:** Repeatedly extract unsettled `u = EXTRACT_MIN(Q)`, add `u` to `S`, and apply `RELAX(u, v, w)` to every outgoing edge `(u, v)`. **Complexity:** **`O((V + E) log V)`** with binary min-heap (`O(V²)` with array).
- **Worked Trace (`s = A`; edges `A→B:4`, `A→C:1`, `C→B:2`, `B→D:1`, `C→D:5`):**

| Step | Settled `u` | `dist[A]` | `dist[B]` | `dist[C]` | `dist[D]` | Relaxations Triggered |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Init | — | **`0`** | `∞` | `∞` | `∞` | — |
| **1** | **`A`** | `0` | `4` | **`1`** | `∞` | `A→B (4)`, `A→C (1)` |
| **2** | **`C`** | `0` | **`3`** | `1` | `6` | `C→B (1+2 = 3 < 4)`, `C→D (1+5 = 6)` |
| **3** | **`B`** | `0` | `3` | `1` | **`4`** | `B→D (3+1 = 4 < 6)` |
| **4** | **`D`** | `0` | `3` | `1` | `4` | Final distances: `A:0, C:1, B:3, D:4` |

### b) Short Note on Topological Sorting [3 Marks]

- **Definition:** A **topological sort** of a **Directed Acyclic Graph (`DAG`)** `G = (V, E)` is a linear ordering of all vertices such that for every directed edge **`u → v`**, vertex `u` appears **strictly before** `v` in the sequence (impossible if `G` contains a directed cycle).
- **Two `Θ(V + E)` Algorithms:**
  1. **Kahn's In-Degree Algorithm (`BFS`):** Repeatedly dequeue vertices with `indegree == 0`, append to output, and decrement neighbors' in-degrees (if output count `< |V|`, a cycle exists).
  2. **DFS Finish-Time Method:** Run `DFS` and push each vertex onto a stack upon finishing (`BLACK`), reading the stack top-to-bottom.
- **Applications:** Build systems (`Makefile`), course-prerequisite scheduling, and spreadsheet formula evaluation.

back: Merge sort does the same work whatever the input order, so it is not adaptive; its O(n log n) never improves on sorted data. It is comparison based, stable and not in place.

back: Randomized quick sort picks the pivot uniformly at random, which makes the O(n²) case very unlikely whatever the input order. A fixed end-element pivot does not have that guarantee.

back: Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly extracts the maximum into a growing sorted region, which resembles inserting items into a sorted part one at a time. Its structure is nearest to insertion sort.

back: Selection sort swaps once per pass and there are n-1 passes, so at most n-1 swaps are made. That low swap count is its main advantage over bubble sort.

back: Insertion sort scans an already sorted array once, shifting nothing, so its best case is O(n). Quick and heap sort still do O(n log n) work.

back: In the worst case, a reverse-sorted array, bubble sort swaps once for every pair of positions, giving n(n-1)/2 swaps. That equals the number of inversions in the array.

back: Quick sort partitions around a pivot and recurses on the two parts, which is divide and conquer. Dynamic programming and greedy methods are different strategies.

back: Heap sort builds the heap in O(n) and performs n extractions at O(log n) each, giving O(n log n) in every case with only O(1) extra space.

citationLabel: Quiz bank · Algorithms · Unit 2 (Sorting) · key C

back: Counting sort builds a frequency array of size k and scans the n items, so the time is O(n + k). It works only for integer keys in a known range.

back: Heap sort rearranges the array itself, needing only O(1) auxiliary space, and guarantees O(n log n) in all cases. Merge sort, by contrast, needs O(n) extra space.

back: Merging needs a temporary buffer holding up to n elements, so merge sort uses O(n) auxiliary space. The recursion stack adds only O(log n).

back: Heap sort is not stable, because sifting elements around the heap can reverse the relative order of equal keys. Merge, insertion and bubble sort are stable.
